title: Relationship of Physical Frailty to Phosphocreatine Recovery in Muscle after Mild Exercise Stress in the Oldest-Old Women

sections.abstract:
Physical frailty is a clinical syndrome associated with aging and manifesting as slowness, weakness, reduced physical activity, weight loss, and/or exhaustion. Frail older adults often report that their major problem is “low energy”, and there is indirect evidence to support the hypothesis that frailty is a syndrome of dysregulated energetics. We hypothesized that altered cellular energy production underlies compromised response to stressors in the frail.

We conducted a pilot study to assess muscle energetics in response to a mild isometric exercise challenge in women (n=30) ages 84–93 years. The frailty status was assessed by a validated physical frailty instrument. Localized phosphorus (P31) magnetic resonance spectroscopy with a 1.5T magnet was used to assess the kinetics of Phosphocreatine recovery in the tibialis anterior muscle following maximal isometric contraction for 30 seconds.

Phosphocreatine recovery following exertion, age-adjusted, was slowest in the frail group (mean=189 sec; 95%CI: 150,228) compared to pre-frail (mean=152 sec; 95%CI: 107,197) and nonfrail subjects (mean=132 sec; 95%CI: 40,224). The pre-frail and frail groups had 20 sec (95%CI: −49,89) and 57 sec (95%CI: −31,147) slower phosphocreatine recovery, respectively, than the non-frail. This response was paralleled by dysregulation in glucose recovery in response to oral glucose tolerance test in women from the same study population.

Impaired muscle energetics and energy metabolism might be implicated in the physical frailty syndrome.
sections.introduction:
Physical frailty is a clinical syndrome of aging ( 1 , 2 , 3 ). The definition of a clinical syndrome is a group of symptoms and signs that co-occur and, in combination, identify distinct pathophysiology ( 2 ). Multiple physiologic systems are dysregulated in those who are phenotypically frail ( 4 ). There is a nonlinear association between the number of systems dysregulated and the presentation of phenotypic frailty ( 4 ). Physiologic dysregulations of multiple systems in the frail are hypothesized to be due, in part, to dysregulation of cellular energetics essential for system function and maintaining organismal robustness and resiliency ( 1 , 5 , 6 , 7 ). Indirect evidence indicates that dysregulation of cellular energetics is associated with the development of the physical frailty phenotype, characterized by slowness, weakness, low activity, exhaustion and/or weight loss ( 1 , 5 , 6 ) (Figure 1 ). Figure 1 A conceptual model indicating the multiple levels of etiology of frailty syndrome Fried LP et al., Sci Aging Knowledge Environ., 2005

A conceptual model indicating the multiple levels of etiology of frailty syndrome

Fried LP et al., Sci Aging Knowledge Environ., 2005

Clinically, frail older adults often report that their major problem is “low energy”. Diminished energy availability, potentially due to diminished production of energy at the cellular level, would, in theory, mean that the human organism is forced to operate at less than the “energetic optimum” ( 8 ), leading to diminished multisystem function and resilience (i.e., the ability to maintain homeostasis in response to stressors). Indeed, frail older adults exhibit increased vulnerability to adverse outcomes and altered response to acute stressors ( 1 , 2 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ).

There is additional evidence to support the hypothesis that altered energetics underlie the development of physical frailty. This includes associations of phenotypic frailty with imbalances of hormones involved in energy metabolism ( 9 ), serum glucose and insulin metabolism ( 10 ), and altered resting metabolic rate ( 11 ). In addition, mitochondrial dysfunction might form a part of the biology of the phenotype, an assertion supported by the finding that mtDNA copy number (related to ATP production) is associated with prevalent frailty ( 7 , 14 , 15 ). Direct evidence of energy dysregulation in the frail, compared to nonfrail, is needed to understand whether altered energy production or utilization is truly implicated in physical frailty (Figure 1 ).

Better evaluation of the role of energy dysregulation in physical frailty requires analysis under dynamical conditions where the system is challenged by a stimulus and the characteristics of its response are measured ( 12 , 13 , 16 ). This approach adheres to the theory of complex dynamical systems, where function at a suboptimal level may only be revealed under stress ( 5 , 12 , 16 ).

We report here on a pilot study designed to directly measure muscle energetics in response to a mild physiological exercise challenge in frail, prefrail, and nonfrail oldest-old women. In vivo phosphocreatine (PCr) recovery (as an index of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and energy repletion after exercise) was measured following the modest challenge of isometric contraction to test the hypothesis that PCr recovery will be more impaired in the frail women, compared to prefrail and nonfrail. We also examine the results from a glucose tolerance test conducted in the same overall population, with a substantial overlap of participants, in order to offer evidence of parallel dynamics in another part of the energy regulation system ( 10 ).
sections.methods:
Study participants were originally recruited to the Women's Health and Aging Study (WHAS) II in 1994 from women 70–79 years in Baltimore who were among the two-thirds least disabled older women living in the community. The sampling frame was of women 65 years and older identified from a random sample selected from the Health Care Financing Administration's Medicare Eligibility list for Baltimore, MD. From within this sampling frame, 436 women aged 70–79 years with difficulty in zero or one of four domains of physical function ( 2 ) were recruited and enrolled in the Women's Health and Aging Study II, a longitudinal population-based cohort study. They received a baseline examination and then six follow-up evaluations at the Johns Hopkins Functional Status Laboratory from 1994 to 2008. At the seventh study visit in 2007–2008, participants were invited to enroll in a sub-study in which P31 magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) was performed. Women with any metallic implants or cardiac pacemakers were ineligible to participate. Out of 153 women evaluated in the seventh exam, 50 participants were eligible, and were enrolled in this sub-study, which occurred from June to September 2008. Of these, only 30 participants had analyzable P31 spectra. A 75g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) was also conducted from May 2008 to March 2009 in 73 women aged 84–95 years. Women with a history of diagnosed diabetes or taking corticosteroids were ineligible for that study. 35 women participated in both the MRS and OGTT studies, of which 22 women had analyzable P31 spectra (7 non-frail, 11 pre-frail, and 4 frail). The Johns Hopkins University Institutional Review Board approved the study, and all participants gave informed consent.

Physical frailty status was assessed at the seventh exam, based on the original theory of a phenotype of dysregulated energetics and operationalization and validation in the Cardiovascular Health Study (CHS) ( 1 , 2 ), with further validation in the Women's Health and Aging Studies where it was also shown to behave in a manner consistent with a clinical syndrome ( 2 ). Five criteria were assessed: weakness (grip strength equivalent to the lowest quintile in CHS, by gender and body mass index (BMI) strata), slowness (walking speed equivalent to the lowest quintile in CHS, by gender and height strata), low physical activity (activity level in kilocalories per week equivalent to the lowest quintile in CHS, by gender), exhaustion or poor endurance (self-reported low energy), and weight loss (BMI < 18.5 kg/m2 or 5% annual weight loss). Those with zero criteria were categorized as nonfrail, those with one or two criteria as prefrail, and those with three or more criteria as frail ( 1 ).

Participants were examined using P31 MRS with a 1.5T magnet (Philips Healthcare, Netherlands). The tibialis anterior muscle was localized with a surface coil. Participants were positioned supine in the magnet bore, with the dominant leg immobilized in a lexan frame with a non-ferrous force transducer compatible with isometric testing in the magnetic field, as described in detail elsewhere ( 24 ). Spectra were obtained at rest for 4.5 minutes, followed by 30 seconds of maximal isometric exertion of the dominant leg, and five minutes of recovery. The 30-second exertion period involved performing isometric contraction with maximal effort by pulling against the force plate into dorsiflexion with the dominant foot. MR spectra were continuously collected every 1.875 seconds. A total of 320 spectra were collected over 10 minutes using the following scan parameters: repletion time 1.875 s, minimum echo time (TE∼0ms), 512 complex data points,1.5 kHz receiver bandwidth.

Performing P31 MRS during the exercise protocol was challenging in these oldest-old women. For many participants, it was difficult to localize the surface coil to the muscle due to the greatly reduced muscle mass in these oldest-old individuals. Combined with variations in coil loading, the low muscle mass resulted in signal-to-noise ratios that were too low for spectral analysis in 20 of the 50 participants.

To enhance the signal-to-noise ratio, every consecutive four spectra were averaged (effective temporal resolution 7.5 seconds). Spectral analysis was performed with in-house software ( 25 ) written in Matlab (The Mathworks Inc., Natick, MA). All spectra were processed with a 2-Hz exponential line broadening filter, and the complex data were fitted to obtain the area under the PCr and inorganic phosphate (Pi) peaks. A mono-exponential model was fitted to the PCr peak levels, PCr(t), during the time interval between the trough of the PCr level and the fully recovered PCr level: PCr(t) = Pmin + (P0 — Pmin) (1 — exp(−kt)), where PCr(t) is the PCr level at time t since the minimum PCr value, Pmin; P0 is the fully recovered PCr level; and k is the rate constant depicting the recovery rate after the exercise ( 26 ). The estimation of rate constant k (1/sec) was done using non-linear least squares. The rate constant k is commonly used as a measure of the efficiency of the oxidative phosphorylation process, since k is linearly dependent on oxidative capacity ( 24 , 27 ). We also computed time to recovery as 3/k (sec), which corresponds to a 95% recovery of PCr levels after the mild exercise stressor.

We evaluated differences in PCr recovery time during the recovery phase for frail, compared with non-frail and prefrail, subjects, using a linear trend test; these differences were also evaluated after adjusting for age.

We also compared the PCr dynamics with stress response by another measure from a separate sub-study (N=73) in the same study population: the 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), the results of which were previously reported by Kalyani et al ( 10 ). In the OGTT study, there were 17 non-frail, 47 pre-frail, and 9 frail women. Here we qualitatively compared the area-under-the-curve (AUC) of the glucose response curve to the time to recovery of PCr, among nonfrail, prefrail and frail oldest old women, to test the hypothesis that the dysregulation of muscle energetics parallels the dysregulation in glucose metabolism in response to a glucose tolerance test. The area under the curve expresses the overall glucose load that the body experiences. Physiologically, lower AUC indicates less glucose load, while higher levels and longer exposure to elevated levels is known to be physiologically adverse ( 28 ). The motivation behind comparing GTT results with PCr recovery is to assess the similarity in response to stressors of two different — but related — systems, muscle energetics and glucose metabolism, as a function of physical frailty status.

Because the final sample with high quality MRS data included 30 participants, we evaluated whether the missingness was random in two different ways: by comparing the characteristics of the 20 women with unanalyzable spectra data to the entire sample of 50 women; and by comparing the 20 women with unanalyzable spectra data to the 30 women with analyzable spectra data.

After visual examination of the MRS data, 20 MRS studies had low signal-to-noise ratio and were excluded from further analysis. There were no significant differences between the 30 accepted subjects and the excluded 20 subjects, or the aggregate 50 subjects, in terms of health and physical frailty characteristics (Table 1 ), suggesting that missingness was random and non-differential.

Results of the MRS analysis of the 30 participants with high quality data are shown in Figure 2 , showing PCr recovery for one exemplar participant; Table 2 shows mean results for all 30 subjects. Phosphocreatine recovery following exertion, age-adjusted, was slowest in the frail group (recovery time mean ± standard error in the mean = 189 ± 20 sec) compared to pre-frail (152 ± 23 sec) and nonfrail subjects (132 ± 47 sec). The pre-frail and frail groups had 20 sec (95%CI: −49, 89 sec) and 57 sec (95%CI: −31,147 sec) slower phosphocreatine recovery, respectively, than the non-frail. Due to the small sample size in this pilot study, especially with only six women in the frail group, the results did not achieve statistical significance (P-value for linear trend test was 0.22). However, the mean time to recovery estimates do suggest a non-linear effect, with a greater difference in rate of recovery between the frail and the prefrail, compared to pre-frail versus nonfrail. This is consistent with frailty as an emergent state of low levels of, and delayed, energy repletion after a stressor. We did an alternative analysis, shown in Table 2 , where we compared the PCr recovery times in women with 0 or 1 frailty criterion (n=22) to the women with 2 or more frailty criteria (n=8). This difference was 72 sec (95%CI: 7, 137; P-value=0.038).

We also examined the difference in PCr recovery time in terms of individual frailty criteria: slowness, muscle weakness, decreased physical activity, weight loss and exhaustion. Women with muscle weakness had slower PCr recovery by 68 sec (95%CI: 12, 124). Although women with exhaustion also tended to have slower recovery, the difference was not statistically significant, possibly due to small number of women with exhaustion (n=3).

Finally, the slower PCr recovery in the frail group following mild exertion parallels findings from another contemporaneous challenge test in WHAS II participants: a 75-g glucose tolerance test (n=73). Responses to these two challenges, PCr recovery from isometric exercise in this study, and area under the curve (AUC) of glucose levels over time following glucose ingestion after overnight fast (Fig. 3 ), show that there is striking similarity of stress response in frail, compared to prefrail and nonfrail, in the two different physiologic systems involved in energy metabolism. In both, recovery time (and therefore increased AUC in Figure 3b ) is prolonged in the frail compared to both prefrail and nonfrail. Age-adjusted AUC was 141.2 mg/dL (± 10.3), 141.3 (± 7.4), and 184.2 (± 13.1), respectively in the non-frail, pre-frail, and frail groups. The difference in AUC between the frail and non-frail, and between the frail and pre-frail groups were statistically significant. sections.discussion:
Consistent with our a priori expectation about the association of physical frailty with energy dysregulation ( 1 ), the results indicate that PCr recovery is 43% slower in frail women, and 15% slower in prefrail, compared to nonfrail women in an age range of 84–93 years. While these trends in lower PCr kinetics were not statistically significant, likely due to the small sample size in this pilot study, they are consistent with the theoretical literature proposing that the physiology underlying frailty is more likely to be observed under stressor conditions than under resting conditions ( 1 , 5 , 13 , 16 ). The data offered here suggest that oxidative phosphorylation kinetics may be dysregulated in frail oldest-old adults, compared to pre-frail and nonfrail, although disturbances in glycolytic metabolism could also contribute to our measures of PCr recovery ( 29 ).

This observation of marked dysregulation in the frail after a challenge are consistent with the results of glucose and insulin response to challenge conducted in the same study population ( 9 , 10 ). However, due to the cross-sectional nature of the study, it should be cautioned that a claim cannot be made that dysregulated muscle energetics is one of the causes of physical frailty. Hence, our evidence is only suggestive. It is possible that there is a common link between PCr recovery and frailty that is age-related; in other words, an unmeasured confounder could explain the association.

This report, though exploratory, suggests that dysregulated cellular energy production could contribute to the dysregulation of multiple physiological systems associated with the frailty phenotype, as well as their mutual regulation of each other, and to diminished robustness required to maintain homeostasis under stress. The dysregulated glucose response to oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) observed in this report and in ( 10 ) could well be a function, in part, of the dysregulated cellular energy production in frail older adults that is the focus of this report. This hypothesis remains to be directly assessed.

The comparison here of muscle energy production in response to isometric exercise with the physiologic glucose response to oral glucose tolerance test in the same study population provides cross-system support for the theory that physical frailty is an emergent state of dysregulated response systems ( 4 ), with compromised recovery from a stressor. It is emergent in the sense that we observe a substantial threshold difference in the state of being frail, compared to being “not frail” (i.e., either nonfrail or prefrail). From Table 1 it is seen that 68% of women were either frail or pre-frail, but this did not correspond well with only 44% of women reporting good or fair health. On the other hand, 88% of the women were “not frail” (i.e. either nonfrail or pre-frail), which corresponds well with 96% of women reporting excellent, very good, or good health. Thus, being frail seems to indicate a markedly greater decline in health than being pre-frail. This is consistent with the theories of complex adaptive systems, where the tuning of the whole operation is driven by energy availability, and adequate tuning creates resilience or robustness in the human organism ( 4 , 13 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ).

Methodologically, the strengths of this study include the study population of oldest-old women living in the community who have been studied longitudinally. This pilot study shows, for the first time, that it is possible to perform dynamic stress-response MRS evaluations in the oldest old (mean-age = 85 yr), some of whom are physically frail. While methodologically challenging, the lessons learned in the actual conduct of the study can offer a basis for further investigation in this area. In particular, the challenges encountered in administering standardized dynamic exercise protocols in these oldest-old women manifested in a substantial number of spectra with unacceptably low signal-to-noise ratio. These challenges could be overcome by using a more powerful magnet, 3T or 7T magnet, rather than the 1.5T that was used in our study. Further improvement may be obtained by collecting spectra at larger time intervals, rather than the 1.875 second interval that we used — which may not have provided adequate time for the magnetization to relax. Use of adiabatic pulse may further improve the quality of spectra.

The limitations of the study include: small sample size; participants being recruited from a narrowly defined sample; cross-sectional design which precludes any causal inference; the number of MRS studies that could be performed was constrained by time and cost demands; and the challenges encountered in administering standardized dynamic exercise protocols in the oldest-old women resulted in 40 percent of spectra with unacceptable low signal-to-noise ratio. Ideally, future studies that build on this pilot study, with experimental protocols geared towards the oldest-old, would have substantially larger sample sizes and would be able to draw definitive conclusions on the role of PCr recovery in frailty.

In conclusion, although the results are not statistically significant, this exploratory study provides preliminary support for the hypothesis that energy dysregulation is a core biologic component of the physical frailty syndrome, and is a key factor in loss of resilience in aging.
